subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. Pankaj came down in his new shirt for the school photo. His elder brother Suraj looked up from his toast. "That colour makes you look ill." Pankaj changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.
Wednesday. Pankaj showed Suraj his science model. "The wiring's messy. It'll short." Pankaj snatched it back and slammed his door.
Friday. The model had shorted in class, just as Suraj said. That evening Pankaj knocked on his brother's door. "You were right about the wiring. But when you say things like that, it sounds like you think I'm useless." Suraj stared. "I didn't mean it that way." "I know. Can you just tell me what's wrong and how to fix it, and skip the 'ill' part?" Suraj nodded slowly, then pulled out a screwdriver.

qa.q: What did Suraj say about Pankaj's shirt colour?
How did Pankaj feel after the shirt comment, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt hurt and criticised; he changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.

qa.q: What choice did Pankaj make on Friday, and what came of it?
qa.a: He told Suraj how the words landed and asked for the fix without the harsh part; Suraj nodded and got a screwdriver.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Pankaj said his words sound like "you think I'm useless"?
qa.a: He seems surprised, since he meant no harm, and may realise his honesty was landing as an attack.

grounding: A teenager hurt by his brother's blunt remarks tells him how the words land and asks for the honest content without the harsh tone.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage: Francis, come and sit by your Aparna aunty. You're sulking because your sister called your haircut a disaster? Let me tell you about my sister Leela. When I was fourteen, she told me my singing was flat, my handwriting looked like ants, and my best friend was using me. Every one of those stung. For a year I thought she hated me. Then one day, after she said my essay was "boring in the middle", I told her, "Leela, when you say it like that, I hear that I'm boring." She was shocked. She said she only meant the middle paragraph. We made a rule: she says the true part, I ask for the useful part. The essay won a prize. And my friend was using me, by the way. So, what exactly did she say about the haircut?

qa.q: What did Leela say Aparna's handwriting looked like?
qa.a: She said it looked like ants.

qa.q: What did young Aparna believe about Leela for a year, and why?
qa.a: She thought Leela hated her, because every blunt remark stung.

qa.q: What turning point changed how the sisters spoke to each other?
qa.a: Aparna told Leela how "boring in the middle" landed, and they made a rule: Leela says the true part, Aparna asks for the useful part.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt hearing Aparna say "I hear that I'm boring"?
qa.a: She was shocked, since she only meant one paragraph, and may have realised her honesty was landing as an insult.

grounding: An aunt recalls being stung by a blunt older sister, telling her how the words landed, and learning to keep the honest part and drop the sting.
